Which IT services companies are getting more out of their people as AI changes how the work is done? 

Our research team looked at 37 listed IT services and outsourcing companies, from Accenture and EPAM Systems to Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys and Wipro. 

For each one, we compared how much revenue each employee brought in this year with two years ago.

Overall, the industry is still growing mostly by hiring. Over two years, revenue across the group grew 6.4% and the number of employees grew 4.2%, so revenue per employee rose just 2.1%. That matters because clients are already pushing for lower prices, and some are asking for discounts of up to 40% when contracts come up for renewal.

The results vary widely by company. Mid-sized firms such as Netcompany, Persistent Systems and Nagarro, along with Accenture and EPAM, are growing faster than most of the group and getting more from each employee. 

The large firms that do most of their work from India, including TCS, Infosys, HCLTech and Cognizant, are improving, but slowly. Wipro, Mphasis, Genpact and Hexaware Technologies now bring in less per employee than they did two years ago.

The full analysis has charts for all 37 companies and explains what the numbers can and can’t tell us: https://lnkd.in/g4yZ6CPy

Imagine you're hiring a senior AI engineer in Dubai.

You've got a great salary on offer, an interesting project, a strong team and you're ready to start interviewing.

Theres just one small problem, the person you really want is currently working for a tech company in London.

They're earning good money. Their partner has a decent job. The kids are settled in school. They've just bought a house.

Now you're asking them to pack all that up and move 3,000+ miles away.

Suddenly, your brilliant job opportunity has got some fairly serious competition and thats before we even get onto the other companies trying to hire the same person.

Businesses spend a lot of time thinking about their competitors. Who's winning contracts, who's expanding, who's offering better products or services.

But when you're trying to recruit someone internationally, your biggest competition might be their mortgage, their partners career or the fact that their kids have finally settled into a school they love.

None of which you can solve by adding another few grand to the salary.

Ive had lots of these conversations over the years, and you quickly learn that the job itself is only part of the discussion.

What would make someone genuinely consider leaving a good position?
Would their partner be able to find work? 
What about schools, housing, the cost of relocating and whether the opportunity offers enough for the whole family?

Sometimes, after all those conversations, the answer is still no.

When you understand what someone actually needs to make a move, you've got a much better chance of putting together an offer they'll seriously consider.

Thats a big part of international recruitment. Knowing how to find the right people is one thing. Understanding what it would take to get them through the door is another.

If you're hiring internationally across AI, Tech or Digital Transformation, Im always happy to have a chat about the talent available and what it might take to attract them.

Following my recent redundancy from Canva, I'm looking for my next opportunity, and it's reminded me just how difficult finding genuinely accessible employment can be.

So many companies advertise flexible working, but still require a few days in the office. For disabled people like me, that can mean being excluded from otherwise suitable roles entirely.

Remote work has allowed me to build a career I'm really proud of.

I spent over a decade in creative production before joining Canva, where I've spent the past five years working across technical business analysis, product operations and creative technology. Much of my work involved managing enterprise systems, improving workflows, supporting automation and responsible AI adoption, and delivering complex projects.

I'm a creative problem-solver who enjoys making complex things simple. Whether that's translating business needs into technical requirements, running pilots and UAT, improving processes, or helping engineers and end users work through challenges, I love finding practical solutions that make people's work easier.

I loved the variety of work I got to do at Canva, but more than anything, I loved the people. I worked alongside some incredible colleagues who were true allies to me as a trans, disabled person. I was also fortunate to co-lead our ANZ Pride Collective (ERG) and contribute to policies supporting LGBTQIA+ employees. That kind of workplace culture is something I hope to find again. 🌈

I'm also passionate about disability rights and advocacy, and have been building on my lived experience through formal training and certifications. I'd love the opportunity to bring that interest together with my professional experience.

I'm looking for full-time or contract roles that are fully remote, particularly in business analysis, technical or product operations, project delivery, and creative technology. I'm also open to other roles where my transferable skills could be valuable, especially in disability advocacy, human rights or social impact.

More than anything, I'm hoping to find an ethically aligned organisation that genuinely supports disabled employees and values what people bring to the table, regardless of where they work.

I need a fully remote role, and I have a lot to offer. 

If you're hiring, or know an organisation that might be a good fit, I'd really love to connect. ☺️

For a while the story about AI was simple and a little seductive. The models would solve everything, and you wouldn't need people in the middle.

It was never quite true, but it was loud, and loud sells.
 
What's become clear over 2026, especially the first half, is how much work sits between a frontier model and a result a business can actually use.
 
Here's the tell.

The frontier labs themselves are the ones admitting it, through their actions. They are building large deployment and services arms, hiring engineers, acquiring companies, pouring investment into the unglamorous job of making their models work inside real enterprises.

If the model alone were enough, none of that would be necessary. The people who build the models are quietly treating the model as the starting point, not the finish line.
 
You can see it in the market too, once you look past the early panic.

A few months ago the fear was that AI would simply wipe out services firms. Since then, some of the largest have had a serious run instead, because buyers rediscovered something obvious. Someone has to connect the model to their data, their decisions, their messy reality. The demand for engineers who can genuinely deploy this, by whatever name we give them this quarter, has only climbed.
 
The commercial shape of it will change, no doubt. The era of contracts for thousands of generic bodies is fading. What's rising is the premium on people who can make AI actually work in one specific business. Offer a company a hundred engineers who can do that well, and they'll take your call today.
 
None of this is a knock on the models.
It's a more honest picture of how value gets created with them.

The intelligence is extraordinary.
Turning it into outcomes is still real work, done by real people.

If you're deploying AI in your enterprise, where does the hard part actually sit for you, in the model, or in everything around it?

What happens when a consulting company gets paid for results instead of hours worked?
It sounds like a better deal for everyone. But I think there's a catch.
Reuters recently reported that major IT services companies are moving toward performance-based contracts as AI makes certain tasks faster and cheaper.
Some customers are asking for price reductions of 25% to 30%, while others want payments tied directly to productivity improvements and business outcomes.
On the surface, that seems reasonable.
If a technology provider promises to reduce operating costs by 20%, why shouldn't part of its compensation depend on actually delivering those savings?
But measuring results is rarely as simple as it sounds.
Imagine hiring a consulting firm to improve customer service.
The firm introduces AI tools, reduces response times, and cuts operating expenses. The numbers look fantastic.
But what if customers are now receiving less helpful answers? Or employees are spending more time correcting mistakes behind the scenes?
The project might meet its contractual targets while making the overall customer experience worse.
That's what concerns me about performance-based pricing.
The incentives only work when everyone agrees on what good performance actually means.
And choosing the wrong metric can encourage companies to optimize the numbers instead of solving the problem.
I'm not against outcome-based contracts. I actually think they could create healthier relationships between customers and service providers.
But they require trust, clear expectations, and a willingness to look beyond the easiest things to measure.
AI will probably make this debate more important across consulting, marketing, software development, and many other industries.
Because completing a task faster doesn't automatically mean completing it better.
If you were hiring an outside technology partner, would you prefer to pay a fixed project fee or link payment to measurable business results?

Abhishek Bartakke is building the alternative. Syncro1 is an outcome-based hiring platform where clients pay only when a placement succeeds, and it is the subject of our new outcome-based hiring interview on TechRecast.

Context: recruitment technology has spent a decade improving the top of the funnel — sourcing, screening, scheduling — while leaving the commercial model untouched. Syncro1's bet is that the model is the real problem.

The hard questions are technical and commercial:
• How do you define and verify a "successful, sustained placement" at scale?
• Where does the AI genuinely do work a rules-based matcher could not — and where is a human still better?
• Pay-on-placement shifts working-capital risk onto the platform. Does that economics hold across a full hiring cycle?

There is also a fair sceptic's question: contingency recruitment has existed for decades. Is outcome-based hiring a structural change, or a modern interface on an old model?

The bigger point: if vendors are paid for activity, no amount of software fixes the misalignment. You have to change who carries the risk.

One thing that stayed with me: Bartakke's argument comes from the inside — HR Business Partnering across high-volume, high-churn sectors where the gaps in traditional staffing are felt most acutely. That is a credible place to have found the problem.

The open question is whether practitioner insight becomes a defensible platform.

There is also a harder question for the platform itself: pay-on-placement is only as strong as the definition of success. If a placement is counted the moment a candidate joins, the model is easy to game. If it requires the hire to stay and perform, the platform carries real risk.

The question is not whether staffing needs better software. It is whether it needs a different contract. Syncro1 Pvt Ltd is a test of whether changing who carries the risk changes how the work gets done.

The UAE issued its federal data protection law in 2021. Five years later, according to published legal commentary, its Executive Regulations are still awaited.
That gap matters more than it seems. Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 already sets out the rights of individuals and the duties of organisations. Much of the operating detail is still missing, and every business handling personal data in the UAE is planning around it.
From a lawyer's perspective, three points deserve attention now:
1. The law reaches beyond UAE borders. It covers controllers and processors in the UAE, and also those abroad that process the data of people inside the country. DIFC and ADGM keep their own data protection regimes, so one corporate group can face several rulebooks at once.
2. It already speaks to AI. Article 18 gives individuals the right to object to automated decisions with legal or serious effects, including profiling, subject to exceptions such as prior consent. As hiring, credit and customer decisions become automated, this short article may turn out to be one of the most important in the law.
3. The clock has not started, but it will. Article 29 gives organisations six months to comply once the regulations are issued. That is a short time to map data, rewrite contracts and train staff. Waiting for the text is a risk in itself.
The institutional picture is moving too. The UAE created a federal authority for artificial intelligence and data in June 2026, which suggests that the two fields will increasingly be regulated together.
My research on digital privacy and cybercrime keeps returning to one lesson: a privacy right is only as strong as the rules and institutions that apply it.
If you run or advise a business in the UAE, what would you most like the regulations to clarify: cross-border transfers, breach notification or the role of the data protection officer?

Over half of enterprise data engineering capacity is spent keeping yesterday's pipelines alive.

That is Fivetran's 2026 Enterprise Data Infrastructure Benchmark, 500 senior data leaders at companies above 5,000 employees. 53% of engineering capacity goes to pipeline maintenance. The average organisation runs more than 300 pipelines, sees 4.7 failures a month, and burns around 13 hours resolving each one. 97% said those failures slow analytics or AI work down.

Fair warning on the source. Fivetran sells managed pipelines, so the ROI claims in that report deserve the scepticism you would give any vendor benchmark. The time split is the part worth sitting with, because it matches what engineering leads say out loud in almost every review I have sat in.

Here is the uncomfortable reading of it. If half the team is on upkeep, hiring does not fix the problem. You are not short of people. You are short of pipelines that tell you when they break.

Most of what gets called a data quality problem is a missing test. Most of what gets called a governance problem is a missing owner. Neither one is solved by a policy document, and both get quietly worse every time a new source gets bolted on under deadline.

So we build the boring parts first. Contracts on the inputs. Tests that run on write, not on complaint. Lineage you can follow from a number on a dashboard back to the row that produced it. One named owner per dataset, a person, not a team inbox. Slower in week one, and the only version still standing in month nine.

How many of your pipelines would tell you they had failed, before a stakeholder did?

Find the signal. Create clarity. Improve decisions.

Something interesting is happening in the consulting industry.
Some of the world's biggest consulting firms are starting to pay much more attention to smaller businesses.
According to the Financial Times, Accenture and the Big Four accounting firms are expanding their services for mid-sized companies, partly because AI is making certain consulting and accounting tasks cheaper to deliver.
I think this could change the industry more than people realize.
For years, sophisticated consulting services were largely associated with major corporations that could afford enormous contracts.
Smaller businesses often had to make difficult choices between hiring expensive outside experts and figuring things out themselves.
AI is starting to change that equation.
When technology can handle more of the research, analysis, and routine work, consulting firms may be able to serve customers who previously couldn't justify the cost.
But there's another side to this.
Smaller consulting firms have spent years building relationships with these businesses. They understand their customers, often provide more personal attention, and can respond quickly when something goes wrong.
Now they're facing competition from companies with much deeper resources and increasingly powerful AI tools.
What interests me is whether technology will make consulting more accessible or simply allow the largest firms to dominate another part of the market.
Personally, I think expertise and relationships will still matter enormously.
AI can help prepare a report or analyze financial information, but understanding why a business operates the way it does requires something more.
And smaller companies don't necessarily want the most sophisticated solution. They want someone who understands their problems and can help solve them.
Do you think AI will create more opportunities for smaller consulting firms, or give the industry's biggest players an even greater advantage?

5 very different problems. 5 Indian AI startups worth knowing about.

This week, #OnTheRadar:

01 | Boltzmann Labs · Drug discovery

Most drug candidates fail, and they fail late, after years of work and a lot of money. Boltzmann Labs builds AI across that process, from designing a molecule to working out how it could be synthesised in a lab, and then runs its own discovery programmes on the platform rather than only licensing it out.

↓

02 | Lexapar · Legaltech

Legal review is usually where a fast-moving company slows down. Lexapar reviews contracts, flags the clauses that carry real risk and lets a company set playbooks so the same question isn't re-argued each time, while being careful to say it is not a law firm and that a licensed professional stays in the loop.

🟢 Built by Rishi Shroff and Atishay Garg | Since 2021

↓

03 | Kombai · Developer tools

A designer finishes a screen in Figma and a developer then rebuilds it by hand. Kombai converts the design into front-end code, grouping elements the way a developer would and splitting it into named components, and it is far less of a language model product than it sounds, with LLMs accounting for under 5% of the output.

🟢 Built by Dipanjan Dey and Abhijit Bhole | Since 2022

↓

04 | Vahan.ai · Hiring

Hiring for blue-collar roles in India still happens over the phone, at a volume no recruitment team can staff for. Vahan runs a voice-first AI recruiter that speaks to candidates in their own language and handles most of the screening, with no app to download and no form to fill in, because every extra step in that journey loses people.

🟢 Built by Madhav Krishna | Since 2016

↓

05 | Cent · Preventive healthcare

Preventive healthcare in India usually amounts to a cheap annual blood panel that tells you very little. Cent sells one annual protocol instead, a full-body MRI, heart CT, DEXA scan and bloodwork turned into an organ-by-organ risk score a doctor talks you through within 48 hours, and customers can't pick and choose which parts to take.

🟢 Built by Shashank ND, Anshul K. and Arpit Garg | Since 2025

↓

How to Run Google Ads for Photographers with AI

One wedding booking is $4,000+ and the couple's friends get engaged next, and most photographers on Google Ads are still paying for clicks from people searching "photography jobs" and "free photo editing app"

{follow Google Ads for Business to learn how to get AI to run Google Ads}

Here's how I'd set up Google Ads for a photographer, then let Claude Code run it:

1. Keywords. Claude calls the DataForSEO API (keywords_for_keywords + search_volume) for your metro and every venue town within 2 hours, then buckets them. Wedding: "wedding photographer [city]", "elopement photographer". Portrait: "family photographer near me", "newborn photographer". Business: "headshot photographer [city]". Phrase and exact only until 30+ conversions.

2. Negatives before you spend $1: jobs, hiring, salary, course, class, degree, camera, lens, editing, lightroom, presets, free, app, stock photos, poses, ideas, captions, clipart.

3. Campaign structure. One campaign per shoot type so budgets don't fight: Weddings (highest intent, date already set), Elopements, Family & Newborn, Senior Portraits, Headshots, and your studio name.

4. Seasonality. December is the most popular month to get engaged, so Wedding inquiries run Dec to Mar. Graduation runs Apr to May. Senior portraits run Jun to Oct. Fall family minis run Sept to Nov. Headshots and newborns run all year.

5. Geography. Couples hire near the venue, not near home, so target the venue towns you shoot in, not a radius around the studio. Set location options to "Presence" only. Claude pulls CDC WONDER birth data by county and bids up Newborn in the counties with the most births.

6. Track signed contracts, not inquiries. Add 3 form questions (event date? venue? budget range?), count calls over 60s, and push retainer values from HoneyBook, Dubsado or Studio Ninja as offline conversions so Google bids for $4k weddings, not $150 mini sessions.

7. Hand the account to AI. Get a Google Ads API developer token, have Claude Code write scripts, run them on a schedule.
Daily: pull search terms, add junk as negatives, pause keywords that spent 2x your target cost per booking with zero bookings.
Weekly: move budget to the campaigns and counties with the lowest cost per booking, write new headlines from winners.
On the calendar: switch seasonal campaigns on the dates above.

8. Guardrails. Every change posts to Slack with a reason. It can't raise budget more than 20% or change bid strategy without approval. You review the log, not the account.

Two Point O Capital (TW.O) has raised $10 million in a Series A round led by Transition Venture Capital, with existing backer Omnivore and angels Chiranjeev Singh Saluja and Sudhir M Reddy also participating. The Bengaluru-based company runs an AI platform that deploys clean energy solutions — solar, battery energy storage, energy efficiency, and wastewater treatment — for commercial and industrial clients across India.

The business model is worth understanding carefully because it's different from most climate startups.

TW.O is not a solar installer. It's not a fund. It's closer to an AI-powered structured finance and asset management platform for clean energy projects. The company uses its own AI and ML stack to do three things: assess which clean energy solution a commercial or industrial client needs, underwrite the project (essentially decide whether and how to finance it), and then monitor the asset performance over time. For the actual installation and maintenance, it works with OEM and EPC partners who execute on the ground. TW.O manages those partners through technology and contracts.

The result is a capital-light model that can scale across geographies without hiring thousands of engineers. The platform does the hard analytical work; the partners do the physical work.

The client list gives a sense of the market they're addressing: Godrej, Wipro, JK Tyre, Phoenix Mills, Premier Energies, Morepen Pharma. These are large commercial and industrial users with significant energy bills, real sustainability mandates, and the balance sheet to invest in long-term energy infrastructure. The C&I segment — commercial and industrial — is the fastest-growing part of India's renewable energy deployment precisely because these customers have both the need and the capacity to act.

The numbers show traction: AUM growing 1.5x sequentially for three straight quarters, 25-30 large customers, and a target of $75-100 million in AUM over the next two years. For a company founded in 2024, that is a sharp ramp.

The investor combination is well-suited to the thesis. Transition Venture Capital is a climate-focused fund — the name says it. Omnivore is one of India's most thoughtful investors in agriculture, food, and sustainability — having them stay in through the Series A is a signal of continued conviction. The angels bring strategic value in energy and infrastructure.

The use of funds covers BESS expansion, solar, energy efficiency, and wastewater — a broadening of the clean energy stack — along with tech development and hiring for the SME segment. That last point is interesting: moving into SMEs means building a product that works at much lower ticket sizes and with much less sophisticated procurement. It requires the AI to do more of the structuring work automatically, with less human intervention. If they can crack that, the addressable market expands dramatically.

India has committed to 500 GW of renewable capacity by 2030. The constraint is not technology — solar and battery tech are cheaper than they've ever been. The constraint is capital deployment: getting the right project in front of the right financing structure at the right time. TW.O is building the infrastructure layer that connects those pieces.

The risk: what happens when a foreign company 'hires' in India without the right structure.

Direct payments to a contractor in India create a taxable India presence for the foreign company regardless of whether a formal entity exists.

PE risk has been enforced against foreign companies in India's IT sector it is not theoretical.

The right structure:
EOR or specialist contract structure eliminates PE risk.
The Indian entity is the EOR.
Your company contracts with the EOR.

With AI rapidly changing workflows, is upskilling still worth the time and investment? 

It’s a valid question. Why spend weeks mastering a new technical process, a complex Excel function, or a marketing framework when an AI tool might automate it tomorrow?

But here is the perspective shift: Upskilling isn't about competing with AI. It’s about learning how to pilot it. 

In operational fields like Admin, Procurement, HR, and Marketing, the nature of "skills" is shifting from static knowledge to dynamic agility:

1. In Admin & Operations: It’s no longer just about managing tasks; it’s about learning how to build cleaner digital workflows and systems.
2. In Procurement: AI can analyze contract data, but it cannot navigate emotional nuances, build trust, or execute complex human negotiations.
3. In HR & People Ops: Data tools can track metrics, but human-centric strategy, conflict resolution, and cultural empathy cannot be automated.
4. In Marketing: AI can generate drafts, but it takes strategic data interpretation, deep audience empathy, and brand intuition to drive actual growth.

Focusing on continuous personal growth rather than absolute perfection helps you stay adaptable. Employers increasingly value real-world capabilities and proactive problem-solving over static credentials. 

I see upskilling as an experiment—testing new approaches, learning from tools, and treating missteps as data for growth. But I want to open the floor to the experts.

To the Recruiters and Hiring Managers: 
When you look at candidates today, how heavily do you weigh recent upskilling vs. hands-on experience? Does a commitment to continuous learning stand out when everyone is leveraging AI? 

Let’s discuss in the comments! 👇

Binance's initial report on the October 29 hack, which affected about $6.34B in assets, lays out an attack path worth studying for any company that runs internal AI tools. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea on October 31.

It started with a fake interview. In September, attackers posed as a hiring company, and in the second round asked an engineer to download a coding assignment to his work computer. During setup, a legitimate pyenv component was swapped for a malicious one, and Binance says endpoint protection did not detect it. On October 20, the attacker used that computer and an internal AI tool to take control of two wallet team members' machines, and found a container deployment token on one of them. On October 29 the attacker used it to deploy a container and reach the transaction signing service.

Then came the part that outlasts a shutdown. Through the signing service, the attacker submitted 50 signed transactions on Ethereum that created malicious EIP-7702 delegations. Those let attacker-controlled contracts move assets independently of Binance's withdrawal system, so pausing withdrawals and shutting down hot wallets did not revoke them. The hot wallets use MPC, with no single complete private key to revoke access, so Binance built a separate process and cleared the delegated code on October 30 with a new authorization to the zero address.

The report does not show Ethereum's signature verification failing. It shows signing permissions being abused. The independent review is still being arranged, and it has to explain how the internal AI tool crossed to other engineers' devices and why existing signing policy allowed the delegations to be created.

For teams that hold deployment or signing power, the systems an internal AI tool can reach belong on the same permission and incident-response list as everything else. Any authorization that survives an app shutdown needs a revocation path that has been rehearsed.

Qantas is cutting about 850 corporate roles and sending work to Accenture teams based mostly in India. Its reason is AI. I think AI is the best reason to keep that work in Sydney.

In my experience working in this every day for the last few years, AI is good at producing work. It is much worse at knowing whether the work is right. It still makes plenty of mistakes and it makes them confidently, or worse, it gets things right but not in the direction you want to travel.

So the work that matters has changed. Deciding what to ask for. Spotting the error before a customer does. Knowing when something is technically correct but wrong for the market. Moving fast when the market shifts. Owning the result when it goes badly.

Every one of those gets harder with distance. Offshoring puts the worker, a contract and a time zone between the business and the person doing the work. Direction reduces, mistakes get missed. When something goes wrong, the accountability isn’t the person sitting next to the team, it’s a contract into a vortex and layers of helpdesk and agreements.

I see this in our own agency. AI has taken on a share of the manual work, it does some stuff really well. It hasn’t touched taste, judgement or oversight. Those are most of what clients pay us for. It works because whoever directs the work knows the client, knows the market and answers for the result.

Marketing is on the Qantas list, which is why I’m weighing in. I’d expect the same to hold well beyond marketing.

Offshoring answered an old question: how do we get work done for less? I think the question now is who is close enough to your customers to direct the work, check it and own it.

About 850 people are caught up in this, most of them in Sydney. None of it is abstract for them. My bet is that within three years some of these companies will be hiring that judgement back. The smart companies will be onshoring, bringing these jobs back home, closer to their users. Those are the companies that will win IMO.

I run a Sydney agency that uses AI every day, so I’m biased but I still think it’s accurate.

Interesting to read about the deals Qantas, Telstra and Coles have done with Accenture (article in comments).

In short, roles in areas like finance, procurement, HR and marketing will move to Accenture, mostly to teams in India, delivering immediate savings. That work is then automated with AI over time. 

1. The business case
Large organisations are stuck with decades of old technology and can’t hire AI talent fast enough, so a partner that co-funds the upgrade is attractive. I’m not an expert, but I’ve worked on enough technology transformations to know it’s not simple.

2. Risks and opportunities generally
The clear opportunity is a faster route to AI capability, with upfront cost shared, for businesses with countless legacy systems. But it comes with an offshoring risk: loss of control over data and processes. Qantas’s 2025 offshore contact-centre breach exposed 5.7 million records.

3. Indirect First Nations employment and procurement risks
Qantas’s RAP commits $45 million in procurement with First Nations-owned businesses and lifting First Nations employee representation from 1.5% to 1.7% by 2028. The risk is that these commitments stay with Qantas, but some of the HR and procurement teams delivering them are moving offshore.

- Employment risk: Fewer entry-level roles (traineeships, graduate, admin), a key pathway for First Nations people, offshore AI recruitment tools that research shows perform worse for some groups, including First Nations people; and loss of local cultural knowledge in HR (e.g. Sorry Business). (Note: AI hiring can be done well. Kmart’s blind AI chat-based assessment led to over 8% of new hires being First Nations, against a market benchmark of 3%)

- Data risk: Indigenous identification data held offshore and fed into AI raises Indigenous Data Sovereignty concerns.

- Procurement risk: automated sourcing can favour past winners and screen out smaller, newer First Nations businesses, and supplier mentoring is hard to offshore.

4. How do we protect First Nations outcomes?
Hopefully these companies, and others exploring similar arrangements, are working with First Nations advisors to consider:

- Writing RAP targets, cultural capability training and data sovereignty protocols into the provider contract and performance measures.
- Testing AI recruitment and sourcing tools for bias against First Nations candidates and suppliers.
- Assessing where First Nations data will sit, and who governs it.
- Supporting affected First Nations staff through the transition.

For Qantas, Telstra and Coles, Accenture may now play an important role in helping them deliver their First Nations commitments.
